To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) auditory stimuli are not necessarily superior to visual stimuli for synchronization; (2) deaf individuals can synchronize with visual stimuli as precisely as hearing individuals, suggesting that crossmodal plasticity can enhance rhythmic synchronization with visual stimuli; and (3) deaf individuals can also synchronize with auditory stimuli as precisely as the hearing individuals, indicating that cross-modal plastic changes can be bidirectional.

the auditory advantage is reduced by the use of a visual stimulus that has a distinct collision point, that deaf people synchronize to flashing visual stimuli better than hearing people, and that deaf people use higher order mechanisms when synchronizing to a bouncing ball.
the auditory advantage for synchronization is more stimulus-dependent than previously reported, and that the ability to synchronize to visual stimuli can improve in deaf individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how auditory and visual information is integrated and processed in the brain and how this integration is affected by sensory experience.
the neural mechanisms of rhythmic synchronization in hearing and deaf populations and the role that experience plays in shaping the neural mechanisms of sensorimotor integration.
the role of experience in the development of human sensorimotor systems and the neural mechanisms of rhythmic perception and motor synchronization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human brain has the potential to synchronize to auditory and visual rhythmic stimuli.
the auditory advantage is not a fundamental difference in processing between auditory and visual stimuli, but a consequence of a complex interaction between stimulus characteristics and experience.
the auditory advantage is not an invariable feature of human sensorimotor synchronization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
auditory and visual timing are both capable of driving rhythmic synchronization, and that the auditory advantage may be reduced or even eliminated by experience and stimulus characteristics.
the auditory advantage is a consequence of a combination of the superior temporal precision of sound and privileged coupling between auditory and motor systems.
auditory advantage in synchronization is more plastic than previously thought and that the auditory advantage can be eliminated or reversed by experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
auditory advantage is not an inevitable consequence of human brain organization, but can be overcome or eliminated by stimulus characteristics or experience.
auditory-visual interactions are highly flexible, and that the asymmetry in rhythmic synchronization between auditory and visual modalities may not be as fundamental as previously thought.

auditory and visual synchronization are more similar than they are different, and that the asymmetry between the two is not inevitable but is instead modulated by stimulus characteristics and experience.
